transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting title: Technical deep dive: multi-region failover + triggers (post-incident follow-up)
Date: 2025-03-20
Time: 3:00pm - 3:52pm PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dev Patel, Owen Phillips, Miles Thornton, Aisha Bello, Mina Haddad
Kestrel Financial: Jordan Kim, Samantha Reyes, Anil Deshpande, Priya Shah

---

Summary (auto-generated)
- Kestrel asked for clarity on Redwood’s current and planned multi-region failover behavior after a recent regional degradation impacting elevated 5xx/timeouts.
- Redwood walked through: current manual/heuristic mitigations vs the in-flight automation program (signal aggregation, trigger engine w/ hysteresis, safe-to-failover checks, progressive failover, and audit logs).
- Key customer questions: what exactly triggers failover, how you avoid “flappy” failovers, what customers will see (HTTP codes, latency, streaming), how Dedicated capacity is handled, and whether failover can violate data residency.
- Agreed on follow-up deliverables: customer-facing behavior doc, diagram of the state machine/safety gates, and client-side retry recommendations.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Incident recap + customer impact
2) Current routing/failover behavior (manual)
3) Region health signals + trigger thresholds/windows
4) Safety guards: capacity, dependency, policy sanity
5) Progressive failover (canary/tiers/routes)
6) Customer-visible symptoms and comms/status page
7) Data residency + Dedicated capacity constraints
8) Next steps

---

[00:00] Dev Patel: Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is Dev from Redwood, Customer Success. I also have Owen from support escalation, Miles who’s leading the failover automation work, Aisha who owns SLOs and alerting, and Mina from the routing team.

[00:16] Dev Patel: The goal today is to answer the questions from the thread after last week’s regional event and give you a clearer picture of what we do today versus what we’re rolling out over the next, call it, several weeks.

[00:28] Jordan Kim: Yep, appreciate it. We’ve got Samantha, our SRE lead, Anil from compliance, and Priya who owns the app integration on our side.

[00:40] Samantha Reyes: Hi.

[00:41] Priya Shah: Hey.

[00:44] Dev Patel: Cool. Before we go deep—Jordan, do you want to summarize what you saw? Just to anchor.

[00:51] Jordan Kim: Sure. We saw elevated 5xx and timeouts for us-east. Mostly the chat completions endpoint. It was around, I think, 18 minutes of pretty bad tail latency, then intermittent errors for another… 30-ish. We did retries but our streaming sessions were dropping. We also noticed some requests looked like they were still being routed to the degraded region even after your status page said “mitigating.”

[01:18] Samantha Reyes: And to be specific, we didn’t see a clean cutover. It looked like some fraction got better and some stayed bad. So we’re trying to understand, is that expected, or was that just the mitigation being manual.

[01:30] Dev Patel: Got it. Owen, do you want to add what we captured from the ticket?

[01:34] Owen Phillips: Yeah, from the support case we pulled traces that matched elevated upstream packet loss on one of the network paths feeding the region. It manifested as timeouts on streaming and some elevated 502/503. The mitigation in that moment was mostly capacity rebalance + routing policy tweaks, but it wasn’t a full region failover.

[01:55] Priya Shah: Can I ask—when you say “routing policy tweaks” that’s like a config change in your control plane? Not DNS, right?

[02:03] Mina Haddad: It can be either. Today we have a few levers. Some are at the application routing layer—our “smart routing” that decides where to send a request based on policy and capacity. Some are edge/DNS based. The exact lever depends on product mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and the failure mode.

[02:22] Jordan Kim: That’s exactly what we want clarified. Like, in plain terms, what’s automatic today, what is manual, and what can we rely on.

[02:31] Dev Patel: Totally fair. Miles, do you want to do a quick “today vs future” overview? Then we can drill into triggers and what you might observe.

[02:40] Miles Thornton: Yeah. So, high-level: today, we have health checks and alerts and some automatic mitigation—like shedding load, tightening timeouts, and some internal rerouting—BUT full region failover is mostly an operator-driven action with checklists. That’s partly because we want to avoid failing over into a worse situation (no capacity, or a dependent service also unhealthy).

[03:05] Miles Thornton: The project we’re in right now is to move from that manual/heuristic process to an auditable automated system. That includes three big pieces:
1) A standardized region health signal aggregator.
2) A trigger evaluation engine with thresholds, time windows, hysteresis, and hold-downs.
3) An orchestrator/state machine that can do progressive failover (like 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%), with safety gates and manual override.

[03:37] Samantha Reyes: When you say “hold-downs,” that’s like you won’t bounce back and forth?

[03:41] Miles Thornton: Exactly. You can think of it as: once we declare a region “failed” for a given traffic slice, we keep it in that state for a minimum time unless an operator overrides. Then we have a separate recovery condition that’s stricter than the fail condition.

[03:59] Jordan Kim: So last week, would that have triggered the new system?

[04:03] Aisha Bello: We can’t say definitively because we’re still tuning, but based on the metrics we saw—tail latency and error rate—yes, it likely would have crossed the “degraded” threshold quickly. Whether it crosses “failover” depends on the safety checks and how long it sustained.

[04:22] Priya Shah: What’s the difference between “degraded” and “failover”? Like do you have levels?

[04:27] Miles Thornton: Yep. The model we’re implementing is roughly:
- Healthy
- Degraded (stay in-region but enable graceful degradation controls)
- Failing (eligible for progressive failover, starting with canary)
- Failed (full failover for that slice)
- Recovering (gradually return)

[04:48] Mina Haddad: And those states can be scoped. That’s important. It’s not necessarily “the whole region is dead so everything moves.” We can scope by route, model family, customer tier, or product surface.

[05:02] Jordan Kim: Okay, but then the customer experience is inconsistent if only some routes move.

[05:08] Mina Haddad: It can be, yes. But the alternative is moving everything, including stable routes, which can cause more impact. That’s why progressive failover exists—start small, validate, then expand.

[05:21] Samantha Reyes: That makes sense, but we need to know what you will do for our account, because we’re regulated and also we can’t have like… half our requests going one place and half another if there are consistency assumptions.

[05:34] Dev Patel: Understood. We can talk specifically about Dedicated as well. You’re on Redwood Dedicated for primary, correct?

[05:41] Jordan Kim: Correct. Dedicated in us-east, burst in us-west. That’s our current setup.

[05:47] Mina Haddad: Right, and that matters. For Dedicated, we also have to ensure the target region actually has headroom and compatible model replicas.

[05:56] Anil Deshpande: And to be explicit, we have data residency constraints for certain workloads. Not everything can go cross-region.

[06:03] Dev Patel: Yep. Let’s park residency for a sec—we’ll come back. I want to make sure we answer the trigger questions first.

[06:10] Jordan Kim: Sure.

[06:12] Dev Patel: Miles, can you explain what signals are used? We’re getting asked internally “what does Redwood consider unhealthy.”

[06:19] Miles Thornton: Yeah. Signals fall into a few buckets:
- Application-level: 5xx rate, 429 rate, timeouts, streaming disconnect rate.
- Latency: p95/p99 end-to-end, and also queueing time (time waiting for a GPU slot).
- Capacity saturation: GPU utilization, queue depth, token/sec headroom.
- Dependency health: like our policy store, auth, model registry, and some upstream network dependencies.
- Network path health: synthetic probes from outside and inside—loss, RTT, and failed handshake rates.

[06:55] Miles Thornton: The “aggregator” normalizes these into a standard contract per region, per service. Then the trigger engine evaluates thresholds over windows. Like, “error rate > X for Y minutes” combined with “p99 > Z” and “probe failures > N.”

[07:13] Samantha Reyes: Can you share the X, Y, Z? Or is that not fixed.

[07:18] Aisha Bello: We can share ranges. We’re careful because fixed numbers can be misinterpreted as a guarantee. But conceptually we’re using multi-window burn rate for SLOs plus some hard safety thresholds.

[07:32] Priya Shah: Multi-window burn rate—like 5m and 1h windows?

[07:36] Aisha Bello: Exactly. Like 5m/30m pairs, sometimes 2m/1h depending on the signal. The idea is we page and/or take action only when it’s both fast-bad and sustained-bad, which reduces false positives.

[07:52] Jordan Kim: So would you automatically fail over on a 5 minute spike?

[07:56] Miles Thornton: Not on a spike alone. We’d likely enter “degraded” and apply graceful degradation first. Failover is gated by multiple conditions and a minimum observation window.

[08:08] Samantha Reyes: Can we talk about the graceful degradation? What does that mean for us? Is that like returning 429s?

[08:15] Mina Haddad: It can mean a few things. For example:
- Tightening server-side timeouts so requests fail fast instead of hanging.
- Load shedding—yes, potentially 429 or 503 for non-critical tiers.
- Fallback model variants if a specific model replica pool is unhealthy.
- Disabling some expensive features like long context if that’s the cause of queue blowup (depending on contract).

[08:40] Priya Shah: Wait, fallback model variants—do you mean a different model than we requested?

[08:46] Mina Haddad: Only if the policy allows it. Typically it’s “compatible variant” you’ve pre-approved, like same family but a slightly smaller quantization or a hot standby. For Dedicated customers we usually don’t do silent model swaps unless it’s explicitly configured.

[09:05] Jordan Kim: We would not be okay with silent swaps. We can handle a controlled fallback if it’s documented and we can opt in.

[09:12] Dev Patel: That’s consistent with how we’re treating enterprise accounts. Defaults are conservative for Dedicated.

[09:18] Samantha Reyes: Back to failover triggers—what about the “safe-to-failover” check you mentioned. What exactly do you check.

[09:25] Miles Thornton: Three categories:
1) Capacity in target region: do we have GPU headroom, is queue depth within bounds, and do we have the model artifacts warmed.
2) Dependency gates: is the target region’s dependencies healthy (auth, policy store, etc.).
3) Sanity checks on the routing policy change: basically guardrails so we don’t route a customer slice to an incompatible region or violate residency constraints.

[09:55] Anil Deshpande: The residency constraint is a big one. How do you encode that? Is it per request or per account.

[10:02] Mina Haddad: Today it’s primarily per account / per route policy. We have metadata about which regions are eligible. The orchestrator will only consider eligible targets.

[10:14] Jordan Kim: So if us-east is sick and the only eligible region is us-east because of residency, what happens?

[10:20] Miles Thornton: Then failover isn’t “safe.” The system will stay in degraded mode and focus on graceful degradation plus operator escalation. We’d also surface a clear reason in the audit log: “no eligible target region.”

[10:34] Samantha Reyes: Okay that’s good, but it also means we can still go down if the region is down.

[10:39] Dev Patel: Right. There’s no magic. If constraints prevent moving, the best we can do is degrade gracefully.

[10:45] Priya Shah: Can we choose to violate residency in an emergency? Like an override.

[10:50] Anil Deshpande: (overlapping) For certain workloads, no. For others, maybe.

[10:55] Mina Haddad: We can support a “break glass” policy but it has to be explicit, and it would be a configuration + approval thing, not something our on-call flips ad hoc.

[11:06] Dev Patel: We can follow up offline with options there.

[11:11] Jordan Kim: Now about “flappy” failovers. You mentioned hysteresis and hold-down. Can you describe in detail? We’ve been burned by systems that bounce.

[11:20] Miles Thornton: Yep. We do:
- Trigger hysteresis: fail condition is “worse” than recover condition. Example: fail if p99 > 2s for 10m AND 5xx > 1% for 10m; recover only if p99 < 1.2s AND 5xx < 0.2% for 20m. (Those numbers are illustrative.)
- Hold-down timer: once you fail over, you must remain failed over for, say, 30 minutes before any automatic attempt to revert.
- Progressive ramp: even if fail conditions happen, we start with a small percentage or a non-critical tier. If metrics improve, we expand; if not, we halt.
- Manual override: humans can freeze the system in a given state.

[12:03] Samantha Reyes: Manual override—who can do that? And is it audited.

[12:08] Miles Thornton: Yes audited. RBAC-controlled. Typically SRE on-call and incident commander roles. Every state transition logs: who/what triggered it, which signals fired, and what safety checks passed or failed.

[12:25] Anil Deshpande: Can we get access to that audit log?

[12:28] Dev Patel: Not directly today as a customer-facing UI, but we can provide excerpts during postmortems, and we’re exploring what we can expose safely. For now we can commit to including the “reason” in incident communications.

[12:41] Jordan Kim: Our question is partly because we need to explain to our internal risk team why it routed one way. So even a report after the fact is fine.

[12:50] Aisha Bello: Internally we also need it for learning. That’s why audit is part of the design.

[12:57] Priya Shah: On the customer-visible side: what should our client expect? Are we going to see redirects, DNS changes, or just higher latency.

[13:07] Mina Haddad: Depends on which path we use. For Hosted API, we can often route internally without you seeing anything except maybe slightly increased latency during the transition. For Dedicated, it can still be internal routing, but sometimes edge/DNS changes are part of the mechanism.

[13:25] Priya Shah: If it’s DNS, what TTLs are you using? Because we’ve got caches we don’t fully control.

[13:31] Mina Haddad: Great question. We are moving toward conservative TTLs for failover records, but we balance that against normal performance and cost. We can share what we’re using in your environment.

[13:46] Jordan Kim: During the incident, we saw no obvious DNS propagation event.

[13:50] Owen Phillips: Right, last week we did not do a full DNS-based regional cutover for your Dedicated pool. It was mostly internal policy + capacity adjustments.

[14:01] Samantha Reyes: That explains the partial improvement.

[14:04] Owen Phillips: Exactly.

[14:07] Dev Patel: Can we talk about streaming? Priya mentioned disconnects. What happens during failover—do streams drop.

[14:14] Miles Thornton: Streaming is tricky because an open stream is tied to the region handling it. If we fail over new requests, existing streams may still be impacted until they complete or time out. We don’t currently migrate in-flight streams cross-region.

[14:30] Priya Shah: So best practice is we detect disconnect and restart.

[14:33] Owen Phillips: Yes. We recommend idempotency keys + resume behavior where possible. And exponential backoff, but with a cap.

[14:42] Jordan Kim: That’s something we can implement. But we need guidance. Like: how long should we wait before retry. Because if you’re failing over, too aggressive retries could amplify.

[14:52] Aisha Bello: Exactly, retry storms are real. We can send recommended client settings. Generally: short connect timeout, moderate overall timeout, and backoff with jitter; plus circuit breaker when you see repeated 5xx.

[15:10] Samantha Reyes: Are you going to return 503 during failover?

[15:13] Mina Haddad: Ideally not, but under severe impairment, we may shed. The goal of progressive failover is to reduce the need for shedding by moving traffic before total collapse.

[15:25] Jordan Kim: But earlier you said “degraded” can include load shedding for non-critical tiers. We are enterprise; what tier are we.

[15:33] Dev Patel: You’re in our enterprise tier; we protect enterprise workloads preferentially in those policies. That said, if the region is fully down and you can’t move because of constraints, you can still see 5xx.

[15:47] Samantha Reyes: Understood.

[15:49] Anil Deshpande: I want to revisit the safety checks. Dependency health—what dependencies are you checking? Is it internal only.

[15:58] Miles Thornton: Mostly internal critical path: auth/token validation, routing policy store, model registry, and some fleet scheduler signals. Also network path health between the edge and the region.

[16:14] Anil Deshpande: If your policy store is global and it’s degraded, would that block failover.

[16:19] Miles Thornton: Potentially yes, if it would make routing decisions unsafe or inconsistent. But we also have “known safe defaults” cached for short periods. This is one of the reasons we prefer progressive failover: we validate that the control plane is behaving.

[16:38] Jordan Kim: This is like a lot of complexity. Where does it live? Is it a service.

[16:42] Miles Thornton: Yes, a centralized trigger evaluation engine plus a failover orchestrator service. The orchestrator owns the state machine and writes audit logs.

[16:56] Priya Shah: And can we query the current state? Like “are we in failover.”

[17:01] Dev Patel: Today, not via customer API. Internally yes; we also post changes to our incident channels. We can coordinate during incidents to tell you the current mode. For bigger customers, we can add that to comms.

[17:15] Jordan Kim: Honestly, it would help if status page had a bit more, like “traffic is being routed to us-west.”

[17:21] Dev Patel: I hear you. We try to avoid over-specific routing statements publicly, but for enterprise we can communicate more directly via support channels.

[17:31] Samantha Reyes: Also, if you do controlled tests—game days—will we be notified.

[17:36] Dev Patel: Yes. For production controlled failovers, we do them in low-risk slices with internal approvals and enterprise comms templates. For your account, we would coordinate. We’re not going to surprise you with a test.

[17:52] Jordan Kim: Good.

[17:54] Aisha Bello: To that point, we’ve been building the alerting around error budgets so we can detect faster without paging unnecessarily. But we also put manual “go/no-go” gates for production tests.

[18:08] Priya Shah: Can you define “low-risk slice.”

[18:11] Mina Haddad: Typically: a subset of traffic by route (like embeddings vs chat), or a subset of customers in a given tier, or a small percentage (1%) of requests. For Dedicated, it might be a smaller pool or a single model.

[18:27] Jordan Kim: For us, chat is the critical path, embeddings less. So you could test on embeddings first.

[18:33] Mina Haddad: That’s a good suggestion.

[18:36] Samantha Reyes: What about model warmup. If you fail over to us-west, do you have the model loaded and KV caches warm.

[18:43] Mina Haddad: Model artifacts, yes. KV cache is per-request context, so that won’t carry over. But we do keep hot replicas. A safety check is “is the target pool already serving this model with acceptable latency.” If not, we don’t fail over into it.

[19:04] Jordan Kim: So cold start could be part of the failover pain.

[19:07] Mina Haddad: Exactly, which is why we verify before moving a lot of traffic.

[19:12] Priya Shah: In last week’s incident, our latency went from ~350ms to like 3 seconds p99. If you’d failed over, would we have seen that p99 drop quickly.

[19:23] Miles Thornton: In theory, yes for new requests, if the target region is healthy and has capacity. But there’s still propagation time—policy updates, edge routing, and client retries. That’s why we want automation to shorten time-to-action.

[19:41] Samantha Reyes: What’s your target time to detect and to take action.

[19:45] Aisha Bello: Internally we’re measuring time-to-detection and time-to-mitigation. We want detection within a couple minutes for major degradations, and first mitigation action (degraded controls) within minutes. Failover is more cautious—maybe 5-10 minutes depending on sustained signals. Again, not a public SLA.

[20:10] Jordan Kim: That’s helpful. We can plan around that.

[20:14] Anil Deshpande: I have a security angle question. Manual override endpoints—are they protected. Are there logs.

[20:20] Miles Thornton: Yes RBAC, SSO, and audit logs for every call. We’re also restricting which groups can override. It’s not open to every engineer.

[20:33] Anil Deshpande: Okay.

[20:35] Dev Patel: Jordan, you also asked about “why did we not fail over sooner.” Can we address that explicitly.

[20:42] Jordan Kim: Yes please.

[20:44] Owen Phillips: In that incident, the early signals were noisy. Error rate wasn’t uniformly high; it was spiky. Latency was high but not across all routes. The team was concerned that a full failover would overload us-west because we were already close on headroom for your specific model pool.

[21:06] Samantha Reyes: So it was a capacity risk.

[21:08] Owen Phillips: Exactly. That’s why “safe-to-failover” checks are central: if we can’t safely take your east traffic in west, failing over makes it worse.

[21:18] Jordan Kim: But then we were basically stuck.

[21:21] Owen Phillips: Yes, so the mitigation was to stabilize the east pool and reduce packet loss impact.

[21:27] Priya Shah: Could we buy more headroom in us-west to make failover safer.

[21:31] Dev Patel: That’s an option. We can also discuss active-active, but it depends on your workload pattern and cost.

[21:39] Jordan Kim: We might need to. Our leadership is asking for stronger guarantees.

[21:44] Dev Patel: Understood. Mina, can you talk about how progressive failover would work for Kestrel Dedicated in particular.

[21:52] Mina Haddad: Sure. In the design we’re implementing, each Dedicated customer can have a “failover policy” that specifies eligible regions and the ramp steps. Example: if east is failing, we move 1% of new requests to west for a specific route/model. We watch p95/p99 and error rate in west for that slice. If stable, we go 10%, then 25%, etc.

[22:20] Mina Haddad: We can also do by customer tier, but for Dedicated it’s more “by account” because the pool is reserved. The key is we must have reserved or burst capacity in the target.

[22:33] Samantha Reyes: Do you do this with connection draining? Like stop sending new traffic but allow old to finish.

[22:38] Mina Haddad: Yes, we’d stop sending new requests to the impaired region for that slice. In-flight requests may still be there.

[22:48] Priya Shah: So we could see a mix during transition.

[22:51] Mina Haddad: Correct, especially for streaming.

[22:55] Jordan Kim: What about idempotency and duplication. If we retry and you fail over, could we get duplicates.

[23:01] Owen Phillips: If you retry a non-idempotent operation without idempotency keys, yes you can get duplicates. We recommend idempotency keys on non-streaming calls where possible.

[23:12] Priya Shah: We don’t use idempotency keys today for chat. We can add.

[23:16] Dev Patel: We’ll send guidance.

[23:19] Samantha Reyes: On the monitoring: can we get signals that a failover happened? Like headers.

[23:24] Mina Haddad: That’s a good idea. We’ve discussed adding response headers indicating serving region. Some customers already infer from trace IDs, but headers would be simpler. Not promised, but we can take it as feedback.

[23:39] Jordan Kim: That would help us. Even if it’s optional.

[23:43] Dev Patel: Noted.

[23:45] Aisha Bello: One thing to add: the new dashboards we’re building include customer impact by tier and by route. So internally we’ll know quickly if enterprise traffic is taking the hit.

[23:58] Samantha Reyes: That’s great, but again, can you share anything externally.

[24:03] Dev Patel: In an incident, we can provide direct updates via support escalation. We can’t expose the internal dashboard, but we can share the relevant details.

[24:13] Anil Deshpande: Can we talk about how you communicate. Status page last week was, no offense, a bit vague.

[24:19] Dev Patel: Fair feedback. Our public status page is intentionally broad. For enterprise we can do more direct comms: what regions impacted, what mitigations underway, and ETA to next update. We’re also building templates for controlled tests.

[24:36] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[24:37] Dev Patel: Let’s switch to “what will you see” in different states.

[24:41] Miles Thornton: In “degraded” state, you might see:
- increased latency but fewer timeouts because we tune timeouts
- potentially more 429/503 if we shed load (less likely for enterprise)
- possible fallback to alternate model pool if configured

[24:59] Miles Thornton: In “progressive failover,” you might see:
- some fraction of requests served from another region (latency profile changes)
- brief transient errors as routing policies converge
- streaming: more disconnects if the impaired region is still serving those streams

[25:19] Miles Thornton: In “failed over” state, ideally:
- new requests mostly stable, but latency may be slightly higher due to distance
- you may notice different IP ranges (depending on the path)

[25:34] Priya Shah: Different IP ranges matters for us. We have outbound allowlists.

[25:38] Jordan Kim: Good catch. Our firewall rules assume us-east egress.

[25:43] Mina Haddad: That’s important. If you have strict allowlists, failover can break connectivity even if we’re healthy. We need to capture your allowlist requirements and ensure both regions are permitted.

[25:57] Anil Deshpande: For regulated traffic, we can allowlist both, but we need to document it.

[26:03] Dev Patel: Action item: Jordan, can you send your current egress/allowlist constraints.

[26:08] Jordan Kim: Yes.

[26:10] Samantha Reyes: Another question: do you have “monitor-only” mode. Like the triggers evaluate but they don’t act.

[26:16] Miles Thornton: Yes. That’s exactly how we’re rolling this out. We run the trigger engine in monitor-only first, compare what it would have done, then gradually allow actions for low-risk slices.

[26:32] Samantha Reyes: Good. We do that too.

[26:35] Priya Shah: Is there a way for us to opt into an earlier rollout? Like we’re willing to be a design partner.

[26:41] Dev Patel: Potentially, yes, but we have to balance risk. We can discuss if there’s a low-risk surface like embeddings to start.

[26:50] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[26:52] Anil Deshpande: If you do controlled tests, do you generate a report.

[26:57] Dev Patel: Yes, we do post-test analysis: timelines, observed impact, alert behavior, gaps, follow-ups. We can share a sanitized version.

[27:08] Jordan Kim: That would be useful.

[27:10] Aisha Bello: Also, we’re correlating failover actions with error budget impact, so we can say “this action improved burn rate” or “this action caused secondary issues.”

[27:24] Samantha Reyes: Great.

[27:26] Priya Shah: I have one more thing: if west is serving, are you still within the same latency SLO? Our end users are mostly east coast.

[27:34] Aisha Bello: The multi-region availability SLO is about being available, not necessarily meeting the same latency. We do have latency SLOs, but cross-region will typically increase baseline.

[27:48] Jordan Kim: So failover may keep us up but slower.

[27:51] Dev Patel: Correct. That’s the tradeoff: “degraded but available.”

[27:56] Samantha Reyes: That’s acceptable if it’s predictable and not 10 seconds.

[28:00] Mina Haddad: Exactly. That’s why capacity checks and progressive ramp are key.

[28:05] Jordan Kim: Okay, can you speak to what you’re doing to reduce detection time. Last week felt like… we noticed before you did.

[28:13] Aisha Bello: That’s part of the initiative. We’re standardizing signals and improving synthetic probes. In some incidents, customer traffic patterns show issues earlier than our aggregate. So we’re adding route-level and customer-tier slicing in the health evaluation.

[28:32] Samantha Reyes: Like per model.
